Photograph: Evan Garcia/Reuters View image in fullscreen Rhossi, a critically endangered Kemp's ridley sea turtle, is prepared to undergo a CT scan at the Houston zoo in Texas on 11 August. Photograph: Evan Garcia/Reuters Texas Rhossi, a rare sea turtle, recovers after 5,000-mile trek from Wales to Texas Kemp’s ridley sea turtle, near death on Welsh beach in 2023, is thriving in Houston despite lingering pneumonia Ramon Antonio Vargas Mon 17 Aug 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 08.34 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Kemp’s ridley sea turtle native to the Gulf of Mexico is largely thriving after he was found nearly dead on a beach in Wales in late 2023, nursed back to health and then flown to Houston recently to continue recovering – though scans revealed signs that the creature has been grappling with lingering pneumonia, according to his caretakers. Rhossi’s condition was detailed in a blogpost on Friday from the Houston zoo, whose veterinary team was tasked with caring for the creature – believed to be no older than age four – and giving him the best chance possible at an eventual, successful return to the wild. Hundreds of sea turtles are stranded in Cape Cod each year. An ‘amazing network’ has mobilized to help Read more Belonging to one of the world’s most endangered sea turtle species, a local dog discovered a 2lb (0.9kg), cold-stunned Rhossi on a beach in a Welsh village in December 2023. Rhossi was about 5,000 miles (8,000km) from the Mexican and US Gulf coast region where Kemp’s ridley sea turtles are native – and from where they have been known to be swept away for vast distances, including across the Atlantic Ocean , by powerful marine currents. Wales’ Anglesey Sea zoo subsequently took Rhossi in and spent the next two years nursing him to health again. His frame had more than tripled, and he had bulked up to 46lbs (21kg) before he took a helicopter ride from Wales to London’s Heathrow airport – and then a transatlantic flight to Houston on 10 August. The Houston zoo’s sea turtle staff by then had committed to taking over the administration of Rhossi’s recovery, the facility said in its blogpost on Friday. And after an initial evaluation, Rhossi’s caretakers placed him in a deep-water tank to let him become acclimated to his new surroundings. Video of Rhossi, a Kemp’s ridley sea turtle who was nursed back to health after drifting from the Gulf of Mexico to Wales. Rhossi then had a more comprehensive medical examination performed by Dr Joe Flanagan, a senior veterinarian who briefly came out of retirement for the assessment, the Houston zoo said. The resilient turtle had his organ function, eyes, mouth, shell and flippers checked. He also had X-rays and a CT scan to take a closer look at his lungs, according to the Houston zoo. Rhossi largely acquitted himself as “healthy, active and vigorous” during the examination, the facility reported. “He’s very strong,” Flanagan said in a Reuters video report . “He swims normally. He dives. He surfaces. He breathes fine.” View image in fullscreen A Houston zoo employee shines a light on Rhossi as the turtle lies on an exam table in Houston, Texas, on 11 August. Photograph: Evan Garcia/Reuters But, after having endured the north Atlantic’s perilously frigid waters prior to his rescue, “his scans revealed a concern for lingering pneumonia”, and his return to the Gulf of Mexico would evidently “take a little longer than expected”, the zoo wrote. The zoo nonetheless added: “Rhossi’s medical team will continue to monitor him and provide additional treatment, as needed, to ensure the best possible chance of a successful return to the wild.” Florida sets record for sea turtle nests but Trump move could stall recovery Read more Houston’s zoo said Rhossi’s story illustrated the “incredible dedication and careful coordination of … multiple agencies and non-profit organizations”. The facility specifically mentioned the US Fish and Wildlife Service, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration , the Anglesey Sea and Houston zoos, the Texas state aquarium and the Welsh helicopter pilot Darren Briggs. Underlying those entities’ efforts is the fact that the population of nesting Kemp’s ridley females is estimated to be only between 7,000 and 9,000, according to the Sea Turtle Conservancy . The US government furthermore has considered Kemp’s ridleys as endangered since 1970, at risk of extinction within the foreseeable future because of threats from humans such as egg collection and killing for products such as meat, information from the conservancy says. Frankie Hobro, the Anglesey Sea zoo director and owner, expressed high hopes for Rhossi as he settled into the Houston phase of his recovery. “It looks like in a couple of years, he’ll be fit for breeding out in the wild,” Hobro said in the Reuters video. “So that’s really exciting news for us.” Explore more on these topics Texas Wales Marine life Animals Wildlife Reptiles Zoos news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

Indiana flooding in photos Rebel Creamery bankruptcy Tropical Storm Lala slams Hawaii Shooting at Kentucky park SCOTUS emergency docket Virginia State shooting Gen Z loves sports betting Looming Social Security crisis Shells from World War II on the ground in Le Porge, south-western France on Monday. - Romain Perrocheau/AFP/Getty Images Hundreds of World War II shells and munitions have been discovered in the French village of Le Porge , as residents return to the ravaged community in the wake of last month's blazes, according to local authorities. Explosions were heard near the village in France's Gironde region following the devastating fires, which swept through the country's southwest. "A bomb disposal operation was carried out today with Civil Protection specialists, recovering more than 400 shells and munitions," a statement from the local authority said Monday. Advertisement Advertisement As the flames approached the community in July, the majority of the village's 3,500 residents were forced to flee their homes, as hundreds of firefighters were deployed to tackle blazes more violent and unpredictable than in previous years. Temperatures in Central and Eastern Europe are soon expected to be 10 to 15 degrees Celsius (18 to 27 degrees Fahrenheit) above normal, as fires continue to spread in Greece and Italy. In Hungary, the country's sole nuclear power station was "millimeters" away from shutting down early Tuesday due to low water levels in parts of the Danube River, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said. Elsewhere, Austria recorded its highest ever temperature on Tuesday at 40.8 degrees Celsius (105.4 degrees Fahrenheit), the country's weather service said, citing a provisional measurement. Europe has always experienced wildfires, but scientists are clear that climate change is making them increasingly extreme . The fires in France have so far burned more than 160,000 hectares (about 617 square miles), making them the largest on record for the country. Upon returning to the scorched community, officials in Le Porge made a startling discovery. Despite World War II ending more than 80 years ago, unexploded munitions are still littered throughout the continent and frequently discovered or unearthed decades later. Bomb disposal experts work on a site after the discovery of shells from World War II in a neighborhood of Le Porge on Monday. - Romain Perrocheau/AFP/Getty Images French President Emmanuel Macron said last month, "The situation we are dealing with today is the most severe we have ever recorded, the toughest since the Second World War." Advertisement Advertisement "Following the fires, explosions were heard, and we responded last week, and we found this field and removed 75 shells," commandant Philippe Delemotte, head of the Bordeaux bomb disposal unit, told French outlet France Info in an interview Monday. "Here, for instance, you've got two mortar shells, a French mortar shell and some German 5 (centimeter) shells," he said. It is unclear why the munitions went undetected for so long, but Delemotte said the heat caused several of the buried shells to explode, alerting authorities to their location. Officials quickly established an exclusion zone due to the risk to the public, with Delemotte saying an explosion could potentially send "lethal fragments" flying several hundred meters through the air. 'Everything burned' On Monday, Gironde region's prefect Sophie Brocas authorized residents to return to affected neighbourhoods after a safety assessment was conducted. Fires are still active in nearby coastal areas but remain "contained," according to officials. Advertisement Advertisement Asked about the discovery of the wartime ammunition, Delemotte said authorities do "sometimes come across this, but it's rare because here they're scattered pretty much everywhere." The French official said he believed the munitions were from historic demolition pits. Photos taken on Monday showed residents returning to the charred village and sifting through the remains of their burnt-out houses. A local resident told CNN last month that he lost his home and pets when the wildfire tore through Le Porge. "It was the apocalypse," the resident said. "Everything burned, even the animals." Across Europe, other historic objects have also been revealed this summer due to the record-breaking heat and crippling droughts hitting the continent's waterways. Advertisement Advertisement Some of Europe's rivers have shrunk to such a great extent that long-submerged relics from ancient bones to century-old shipwrecks have been revealed. In Hungary too, where the heat crisis is severely straining the country's energy supply , the receding water levels of the Danube River exposed several bombs, likely from World War II, a local official said last week. Temperatures in the country are soon expected to reach 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit). The Hungarian Meteorological Service is forecasting Budapest to top out at 40 degrees Celsius for three consecutive days, something that has only occurred once before in the city's recorded history, earlier this summer during the major European heatwave in late June. Advertisement Advertisement Magyar said Tuesday that Hungary may need to consider a different type of cooling system for the country's Paks nuclear power plant, instead of relying on the Danube, Reuters reported. Water from the river is used to cool the plant's reactor core and other crucial components. CNN's Taylor Ward, Monica Garrett and Ivana Kottasová contributed reporting. https://hayspost.com/posts/ba348d24-4c4e.text: Prison: Kansas man admits illegally selling advanced technolgy to Russia Post photo KANSAS CITY, KANSAS – A Kansas businessman was sentenced to 18 months in prison for violating United States customs laws by selling advanced aviation technology to Russian end users. According to court documents, Cyril Gregory Buyanovsky, 63, of Lawrence, pleaded guilty to conspiracy and money laundering. Buyanovsky is the former president and owner of KanRus Trading Company, a Kansas-based avionics enterprise. As part of his plea agreement, Buyanovsky consented to the forfeiture of over $450,000 worth of avionics equipment and accessories and a $50,000 personal forfeiture judgment. After Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the U.S. government tightened export controls concerning Russia. Buyanovsky and KanRus vice president Douglas Edward Robertson, 59, of Olathe conspired to continue to purchase, sell, and export sophisticated and controlled avionics equipment to customers in Russia without the required licenses from the U.S. Department of Commerce. Robertson pleaded guilty to export control and money laundering violations and was sentenced to 32 months in prison. “Congress put trade restrictions in place to discourage Russia’s continued aggression in Ukraine. The defendants ignored those laws and saw the war not as a humanitarian crisis, but as a business opportunity to boost their profits,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan A. Kriegshauser. “The sentencing of Mr. Buyanovsky marks the final chapter of an investigation that exposed a deliberate conspiracy to circumvent U.S. export-control laws and facilitate the unlawful transfer of advanced aviation technology to Russia following its invasion of Ukraine. This case underscores the FBI’s steadfast commitment to protecting the integrity of our nation’s export-control system and holding accountable those who seek to undermine it. Our message is clear: The FBI will continue to work closely with our law enforcement and government partners to identify, investigate, and disrupt any efforts to exploit our laws,” said Chris Ormerod, FBI Kansas City Special Agent in Charge. A third defendant, Oleg Chistyakov, a/k/a Olegs Čitsjakovs, 57, of the Republic of Latvia, acted as a broker for KanRus. He was sentenced to 28 months in prison after pleading guilty to his part in the conspiracy. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Department of Commerce’s Office of Export Enforcement investigated the case. The Latvian authorities assisted in the investigation while U.S. Customs and Border Protection provided substantial assistance. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Scott Rask and Ryan Huschka for the District of Kansas as well as Adam Barry, a former trial attorney of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section, prosecuted the case. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs provided valuable assistance.

Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP View image in fullscreen The foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, said it was the first time Australian sanctions had targeted a construction company in the building of illegal settlement in the occupied West Bank. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP West Bank ‘Godmother’ of illegal Israeli West Bank settler project Daniella Weiss among group sanctioned by Australia Foreign affairs minister Penny Wong says rapid expansion of settlements and settler violence are ‘extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution’ Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Krishani Dhanji and Emma Elsworthy Tue 17 Nov 2026 15.20 EST Last modified on Tue 17 Nov 2026 18.43 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Australia has announced another tranche of sanctions on individuals and organisations involved in “illegal settlement expansion and human rights abuses against Palestinians” in the West Bank . In a statement, the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong , said it was the first time Australian sanctions had targeted a construction company involved in the building of settlements. The sanctions prohibit Australians and Australian businesses from trading with or providing financial or other support to three individuals and four organisations. Most Israelis think settlements policy should change to avoid more sanctions, poll finds Read more “We are taking these actions because the rapid expansion of settlements and settler violence are extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution,” Wong’s statement said. “This includes the E1 settlement where demolitions and the displacement of Palestinians have occurred in recent weeks. Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law.” Among those sanctioned is Daniella Weiss and her Israeli settler organisation, the Nachala movement, which the government said has provided support for outposts and settlements that have perpetrated serious human rights abuses. Weiss is known as the “godmother” of the settler movement and was sanctioned by the UK in May 2025, shortly after she appeared on a Louis Theroux’s documentary The Settlers . View image in fullscreen Nachala movement leader Daniella Weiss is known as the ‘godmother’ of the settler movement. Photograph: Erik Marmor/Getty Images Prominent West Bank settler Eliav Libi has also been sanctioned, as well as the Eyal Hari Yehuda construction company which has helped develop settlements and outposts and demolished Palestinian structures in the West Bank. Wong said the sanctioned individuals and organisations had “actively participated in the planning, coordination and establishment of new settlements, including raising funds, recruitment of volunteers and providing support to violent settlers”. Speaking on ABC radio on Wednesday morning, Wong said Australia had been coordinating with the UK on the sanctions. “We thought it was very important to work with the United Kingdom to have a coordinated set of sanctions ahead of those decisions. “We urge Israel to desist from proceeding with this settlement, which renders likely unviable the prospect of a Palestinian state.” View image in fullscreen The E1 corridor in the occupied West Bank, where Israel is planning more settlements. Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty Images Wong said she had spoken to her Israeli counterpart, Gideon Sa’ar, on Tuesday night when she “outlined” Australia’s position. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “We’ve made clear we will continue to take action in respect of those involved in the settlement enterprise. The settlement enterprise is violent.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Wong had signalled further sanctions in September, after the government ruled out an import ban on trade from illegal settlements in the West Bank. On Wednesday, the foreign affairs minister said the government was still considering further action, but provided no detail. Food grown in illegal West Bank settlements being sold in Australia as ‘produce of Israel’ Read more “We’ll continue to look at targeted measures we can take to push back against what the current Israeli government is doing,” Wong told journalists. When asked whether Wong was concerned Israel would respond to Australia sanctions with countermeasures, the minister said it had in the past. “We’ve seen the Israeli government take action against Australia, including asking our diplomats to leave Ramallah. We’ve also seen the caretaker prime minister, Netanyahu, be very public in his criticism of Australia. “So obviously, there is a reaction to Australia acting, but we think this is the right thing to do.” The statement warned Australian businesses they must not bid for construction tenders for illegal settlement developments. Individuals breaching sanctions can attract a penalty of up to 10 years’ imprisonment and a fine of up to $910,000 or three times the value of the relevant transaction. Businesses can be fined up to $3.64m or three times the value of the relevant transaction. https://www.ebrd.com/home/news-and-event.text: EBRD supports major wind farm in Romania 06 Nov 2026 Share Linkedin Facebook Whatsapp Twitter Email Copy Link Author: Anastasia Dolmatova EBRD lending up to €31.9 million to support one of Romania’s largest wind farms Renewable energy generated will meet needs of around 600,000 people, contributing to country’s 2030 wind power target EU providing guarantee and assistance with green skills through InvestEU programme The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) is providing a senior loan of up to €31.9 million to Midmar Callatis, a wholly-owned project subsidiary of Rezolv Energy, to finance the construction and operation of Dunarea East, which will be one of Romania’s largest wind farms. This loan forms part of a broader senior financing package of up to €367 million. With an installed capacity of 292.5 MW, the wind farm is expected to generate 673 GWh of renewable electricity annually, equivalent to the annual electricity needs of around 600,000 people. The project will account for around 4 per cent of Romania ’s 2030 onshore wind capacity target, supporting the country’s energy security and decarbonisation goals. The EBRD financing will benefit from a €7.6 million first-loss guarantee provided by the European Union (EU) under its InvestEU programme, helping to mobilise private investment in renewable energy. The Bank is also working with Rezolv Energy on a skills development programme in Constanța County, supported by an InvestEU-funded technical cooperation grant. The programme will work with local educational institutions to provide accredited training in wind energy and related skills to at least 100 people by 2030, supporting employment in Romania’s growing renewable energy sector. The initiative will also seek to increase women’s participation in the sector, with female trainees expected to account for at least 30 per cent of total programme participants. The programme will include measures aimed at preventing and addressing gender-based violence and harassment in the workplace. This investment comes at a time when Romania is accelerating the deployment of renewable energy to strengthen energy security, diversify its energy mix and support its decarbonisation objectives. By increasing domestic production of renewable electricity, the project will help to reduce reliance on imported fuels and more carbon-intensive energy sources, while enhancing the resilience of the national power system. This project is sponsored by Rezolv Energy, a renewable energy developer backed by Actis and Mubadala. The EBRD has worked with Rezolv Energy on a number of renewable energy investments in Romania since 2024 (including the Vifor Wind project and the Dama Solar project ), supporting the continued growth of Romania’s renewable energy sector and the country’s transition to a more sustainable, secure and competitive energy system. The EBRD is a leading institutional investor in Romania. Since beginning operations in the country in 1991, the Bank has invested more than €12.9 billion across 609 projects, with the majority of that investment going to the private sector. Since 2024, the Bank has invested over €700 million in more than 15 energy projects in Romania, supporting over 4.5 GW of renewable energy capacity. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckz7.text: Image source, FBI Image caption, Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was detained by Mexican special forces on Friday By Tara Mewawalla Published 21 November 2026, 13:15 GMT Updated 1 hour ago A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities. Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores and seven others were detained by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said. Seven suspects were killed in the operation, as were four members of the Mexican army who were travelling to reinforce security in Guasave, the secretariat added. Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition. Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House. Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile. Using US intelligence on his whereabouts, Mexican special forces descended on his location using "stealth and surprise", establishing a perimeter to prevent him from escaping and reinforcements arriving, Mexico's defence secretariat said. However, they "came under attack from gunfire and explosives" before entering the property and arresting Meza Flores, the secretariat continued. Videos circulating online appear to show helicopters firing streams of bullets towards the ground in Guasave. Others appear to show people at a baseball stadium fleeing as they hear shooting sounds. Image source, Reuters Image caption, A number of vehicles were pictured burning on a highway near Los Mochis, Sinaloa, after Fausto Isidro "Chapo Idisro" Meza Flores was arrested Eight people in total were arrested, including Meza Flores' second-in-command, who is also his cousin, and his brother-in-law, who is the group's financial operator, the secretariat added. Meza Flores, his cousin, and his brother-in-law were flown to Mexico City to face prosecution, the defence secretariat said. The other five remained in the state of Sinaloa. Authorities also said they had seized multiple weapons during the operation, including a grenade launcher, as well as drugs and cash. When Meza Flores was added to the FBI's most-wanted list in 2025, he was accused of "heinous crimes" including kidnapping, extortion and torture. Then-acting FBI director Brian Driscoll said Meza Flores and his organisation had also unleashed a "scourge of illicit drugs" into the US via its southern border with Mexico. He was initially charged with drug trafficking in the US in 2012 before being charged again in 2019. The 44-year-old is alleged to have conspired to manufacture and distribute large quantities of cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana between 2005 and 2019. Meza Flores was originally a high-ranking member of the BeltrÃ¡n Leyva Organization, but a split between rival factions led to a surge of violence and prompted him to establish his own cartel by 2013. His organisation has also engaged in what US officials described as an "extremely violent turf war" with the Sinaloa Cartel, one of the most powerful drug trafficking gangs, which operates in the same region. Meza Flores was added to the FBI's most-wanted list after Mexican authorities reportedly linked his cartel to 20 million fentanyl pills they seized in 2024. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has taken a tougher stance on the country's cartels in a bid to resist US intervention on Mexican soil. Mexico has welcomed closer collaboration but resisted US boots on the ground. Trump made stemming the flow of drugs into the US across its southern border one of his key election pledges.
